headline: Sam Altman: OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math discoveries
summary: Despite criticism over communication and attribution, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the company will continue its relentless pursuit of scientific knowledge, hinting at more discoveries to come.
details: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledges the disruption caused by the company's AI-generated mathematical results but insists that humanity deserves fundamental knowledge. He stated that OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions of dollars on tackling mathematical problems, including around $10 million on its Navier-Stokes solution.

Altman sympathizes with mathematicians struggling to keep up with the deluge of AI-generated findings but has no intention of stopping. He believes the public's right to new scientific knowledge outweighs the disruption, emphasizing that major discoveries should not be withheld.

Mathematicians have criticized OpenAI for inadequate attribution, lack of context, and insufficient verification in its announcements. This year alone, OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results, often with brief, hard-to-follow writeups.

Despite the criticism, OpenAI is also facing accusations of gatekeeping research, particularly regarding a claimed breakthrough in Yang-Mills theory, details of which have not been publicly released. The company cites expert recommendations for its new approach to communication.

Altman revealed that OpenAI possesses a stockpile of further mathematical discoveries beyond those already published. He described an internal Slack channel, 'Model Name-Hold My Beer,' where employees pushed AI models to their limits on the hardest problems.

The significant resources AI labs are investing in scientific problems raise concerns among researchers about being priced out of their own fields. Altman's comments suggest that mathematicians hoping for a respite may be disappointed.

headline_marked: Runware aims to [[mass-produce AI data centers]] on an assembly line
headline: Runware aims to mass-produce AI data centers on an assembly line
summary: The company plans to scale production to 30 megawatts per day by 2028, aiming to assemble modular data centers in a factory setting.
details: AI infrastructure company Runware is pushing to revolutionize data center construction by building modular pods on an assembly line, akin to car manufacturing. Their goal is to dramatically speed up deployment and increase efficiency in the rapidly growing AI sector.

Runware plans to scale its Romania-based factory to produce 30 megawatts of data center capacity daily by 2028. This ambitious target reflects a broader industry trend towards faster and more efficient data center deployment, with companies like Nvidia also exploring similar concepts.

Unlike some competitors, Runware claims to have already built a functional factory for pod assembly. They are currently expanding their facilities, with a second factory expected to be operational early next year, reducing pod build time from weeks to a single day.

The company offers flexibility to customers, allowing them to provide their own sites for assembly or have Runware find one. Runware aims to have pods online within 48 hours of arrival on-site, covering installation and setup.

Runware's modular pods are customizable to customer preferences and can be configured for the latest GPU chips. This adaptability is crucial, as it allows Runware to align infrastructure with hardware lead times and even design custom components for new GPU generations.

While the concept is promising, execution remains key. Runware, which has raised over $60 million, faces challenges in scaling operations, managing supply chains, and securing funding for its Series B round. The company has hired an experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to oversee manufacturing.

Despite potential component sourcing challenges, Runware reports significant interest, with $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since they became available to outside customers a month ago.
